issues.legal_issue: A change from a development plan’s designated land-use category must be authorized under the statutory route governing changes from that plan and cannot be granted through ordinary permission where the proposed use is prohibited by the applicable zoning regulations.
material_facts: The land was designated for residential use, and the proposed restaurant use was not permitted in that zone under either category of use in the zoning regulations.
The planning and government authorities approved a change from residential to commercial use, treating the application as one to change the development plan’s designated use.

The approval did not identify any qualifying circumstance necessitating a change to the plan, and the record did not establish the required public-interest basis or compliance with the other statutory conditions.
The planning authority’s officers had identified the prospect of increased traffic and parking problems, but the approval did not explain how those concerns were addressed.
issues.conclusion: The ordinary permission provisions and the provision for changes from the development plan operate in different fields. Because the proposed use was not permitted by the zoning regulations and the statutory requirements for changing the plan were not met, the conversion approval could not stand.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 14(1), 14(2) and 15 of the Karnataka Town and Country Planning Act, 1961 govern changes that conform to the development plan and zoning regulations; they do not authorize a use prohibited by those regulations. Section 14-A governs changes from the Outline Development Plan and requires a specified basis for the change, public interest, consistency with other applicable laws, and publication inviting objections. Section 15(2)’s deemed-permission mechanism is subject to conformity with the plan and regulations under Section 13(3). The court relied on Ashok Leyland Ltd. v. State of T.N. on giving effect to the words “subject to,” and considered Special Deputy Commissioner v. Bhargavi Madhavan and Sri Krishnapur Mutt v. N. Vijayendra Shetty in addressing the statutory scheme.

rule.if: appeal_from_writ_dismissal and land_use_change_from_development_plan and proposed_use_barred_by_zoning and not qualifying_basis_for_plan_change

predicates.appeal_from_writ_dismissal: A party appeals after a court has dismissed a challenge to an administrative land-use conversion.
predicates.land_use_change_from_development_plan: The proposed conversion changes the use designated for the land in the applicable development plan.
predicates.proposed_use_barred_by_zoning: The proposed use is not permitted by the applicable zoning regulations.
predicates.qualifying_basis_for_plan_change: The authorities identify and establish a qualifying circumstance that necessitates changing the development plan’s designated use.

issues.definition: When an appeal follows dismissal of a challenge to a land-use conversion, the conversion is invalid if it changes the plan-designated use to one barred by zoning and the authorities have not established a qualifying basis for changing the plan.

issues.legal_issue: An administrative approval for a statutory land-use change is invalid when the authority fails to address the governing legal requirements and material considerations or gives reasons that do not disclose a lawful basis for its decision.
material_facts: The approval did not state the purpose or grounds for the change and did not disclose how the statutory requirements had been satisfied.
The planning authority’s officers had identified likely traffic and parking problems, but the decision did not explain how those concerns were resolved.
The authority’s reasons did not show that it had applied its mind to the legal conditions governing the change or to the objections and relevant considerations.
issues.conclusion: The authorities misdirected themselves in law by failing to consider the governing requirements and relevant factors; the approval was therefore vitiated and could not stand.
issues.legal_principle: Judicial review may address errors of law and, in appropriate circumstances, errors of fact, including posing the wrong question, failing to consider relevant factors, or considering irrelevant ones. Reasons that are legally bad or substantially inadequate may constitute error of law. The court relied on Hindustan Petroleum Corpn. Ltd. v. Darius Shapur Chenai, which discussed Cholan Roadways Ltd. v. G. Thirugnanasambandam; it also cited Sonepat Cooperative Sugar Mills Ltd. v. Ajit Singh. An administrative order is judged by its own contents, not by explanations later supplied in an affidavit, as stated in Bangalore Development Authority v. R. Hanumaiah.

rule.if: appeal_from_writ_dismissal and administrative_land_use_approval and statutory_requirements_unaddressed and material_concerns_unaddressed

predicates.appeal_from_writ_dismissal: A party appeals after a court has dismissed a challenge to an administrative decision.
predicates.administrative_land_use_approval: An authority has issued an approval changing the permitted use of land.
predicates.statutory_requirements_unaddressed: The approval does not show that the authority considered the legal conditions governing the decision.
predicates.material_concerns_unaddressed: The authority does not address material objections or concerns relevant to its decision.

issues.definition: An administrative land-use approval is quashed on appeal when the authority has not shown that it considered the governing legal conditions and has left material concerns unaddressed.
